claim: The Large Cell (LC) motor neurons of the crab cardiac ganglion have variable membrane conductance magnitudes even within the same individual.
source: The Large Cell (LC) motor neurons of the crab cardiac ganglion have variable membrane conductance magnitudes even within the same individual, yet produce identical synchronized activity in the intact network.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to previous work (Lane et al., 2016; Ransdell et al., 2013a; Ransdell et al., 2013b) mentioned in the introduction.

claim: LC motor neurons produce identical synchronized activity in the intact network despite variable conductances.
source: The Large Cell (LC) motor neurons of the crab cardiac ganglion have variable membrane conductance magnitudes even within the same individual, yet produce identical synchronized activity in the intact network.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated throughout the manuscript with data showing synchronized bursting in control conditions.

claim: Blocking a subset of K+ conductances across LCs results in loss of synchronous activity.
source: In a previous study we blocked a subset of K+ conductances across LCs, resulting in loss of synchronous activity (Lane et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lane et al., 2016.

claim: Both serotonin (5HT) and dopamine (DA) have distinct excitatory effects on LC output.
source: Both amines had distinct excitatory effects on LC output, but only 5HT caused desynchronized output.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased excitability measures for both modulators presented in Figure 2 and the Results section.

claim: Only 5HT caused desynchronized output among the two amines tested.
source: Both amines had distinct excitatory effects on LC output, but only 5HT caused desynchronized output.
evidence: This is supported by R² measurements shown in Figure 3 demonstrating loss of synchrony in 5HT but not DA.

claim: DA rapidly increased gap junctional conductance.
source: We further determined that DA rapidly increased gap junctional conductance.
evidence: This is supported by direct measurements of coupling conductance shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Co-application of DA and 5HT induced 5HT-like output but waveforms remained synchronized.
source: Co-application of both amines induced 5HT-like output, but waveforms remained synchronized.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 5 showing double-bursting (5HT-like) with maintained high R² values.

claim: DA prevented desynchronization induced by the K+ channel blocker tetraethylammonium (TEA).
source: Furthermore, DA prevented desynchronization induced by the K+ channel blocker tetraethylammonium (TEA), suggesting that dopaminergic modulation of electrical coupling plays a protective role in maintaining network synchrony.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing maintained synchrony when DA is co-applied with TEA.

claim: Dopaminergic modulation of electrical coupling plays a protective role in maintaining network synchrony.
source: Furthermore, DA prevented desynchronization induced by the K+ channel blocker tetraethylammonium (TEA), suggesting that dopaminergic modulation of electrical coupling plays a protective role in maintaining network synchrony.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings that DA increases coupling and prevents desynchronization.

claim: Neuromodulation reconfigures network output by altering a subset of cellular and synaptic conductances.
source: One mechanism of providing flexibility to network activity is neuromodulation, which reconfigures network output by altering a subset of cellular and synaptic conductances (Harris-Warrick, 2011; Bargmann, 2012; Daur et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by multiple citations.

claim: Many networks achieve stable output through variable solutions where intrinsic membrane conductances and synaptic strengths can be highly variable yet still produce nearly identical physiological activity.
source: However, many networks achieve stable output by a variety of solutions; intrinsic membrane conductances and synaptic strengths can be highly variable yet still produce nearly identical physiological activity (Ball et al., 2010; Calabrese et al., 2011; Marder, 2011; Ransdell et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The crustacean cardiac ganglion (CG) is a central pattern generator network that produces rhythmic bursts with precisely synchronized activity across all five Large Cell (LC) motor neurons.
source: The crustacean cardiac ganglion (CG) is a central pattern generator network that produces rhythmic bursts with precisely synchronized activity across all five Large Cell (LC) motor neurons (Lane et al., 2016; Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and demonstrated in Figure 1B showing synchronized bursting.

claim: Constituent LCs are variable in many ionic conductances, including A-type K+ (IA), high-threshold K+ (IHTK), and voltage-dependent Ca2+ (ICa).
source: Despite virtually identical output across LCs within a given network, constituent LCs are variable in many ionic conductances, including A-type K+ (IA), high-threshold K+ (IHTK), and voltage-dependent Ca2+ (ICa) (Ransdell et al., 2013a; Ransdell et al., 2013b; Lane et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: When subsets of K+ conductances are blocked in LCs of a network, synchrony is disrupted.
source: When subsets of K+ conductances are blocked in LCs of a network, synchrony is disrupted, although ultimately is restored by a combination of compensatory changes in membrane conductance and electrical synaptic strength (Lane et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lane et al., 2016.

claim: Synchrony is ultimately restored after K+ conductance blockade by a combination of compensatory changes in membrane conductance and electrical synaptic strength.
source: When subsets of K+ conductances are blocked in LCs of a network, synchrony is disrupted, although ultimately is restored by a combination of compensatory changes in membrane conductance and electrical synaptic strength (Lane et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lane et al., 2016.

claim: The CG is modulated by many substances, including neuropeptides and the biogenic amines serotonin and dopamine.
source: The CG is modulated by many substances, including neuropeptides and the biogenic amines serotonin and dopamine (DA) (Cooke, 2002; Cruz-Bermúdez and Marder, 2007) that are known to target the same K+ conductances that lead to desynchronization when altered (Kloppenburg et al., 1999; Peck et al., 2001; Johnson et al., 2003; Gruhn et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Serotonin and dopamine are known to target the same K+ conductances that lead to desynchronization when altered.
source: The CG is modulated by many substances, including neuropeptides and the biogenic amines serotonin and dopamine (DA) (Cooke, 2002; Cruz-Bermúdez and Marder, 2007) that are known to target the same K+ conductances that lead to desynchronization when altered (Kloppenburg et al., 1999; Peck et al., 2001; Johnson et al., 2003; Gruhn et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: 5HT (10−6M) is excitatory when applied to the entire CG of C. borealis.
source: Both 5HT (10−6M) and DA (10−5M) are excitatory when applied to the entire CG of C. borealis (Cruz-Bermúdez and Marder, 2007), and our results recapitulate this same effect (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by citation and confirmed by data in Figure 2.

claim: DA (10−5M) is excitatory when applied to the entire CG of C. borealis.
source: Both 5HT (10−6M) and DA (10−5M) are excitatory when applied to the entire CG of C. borealis (Cruz-Bermúdez and Marder, 2007), and our results recapitulate this same effect (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by citation and confirmed by data in Figure 2.

claim: 5HT significantly increased pacemaker burst duration.
source: 5HT significantly increased pacemaker burst duration, and in 6 out of 8 experiments switched the network to a distinct output consisting of a single prolonged pacemaker burst driving two different and distinct LC bursts that we term 'double-bursting' (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 2A and B showing increased SC off phase.

claim: In 6 out of 8 experiments, 5HT switched the network to a distinct output consisting of a single prolonged pacemaker burst driving two different and distinct LC bursts termed 'double-bursting'.

claim: 5HT modulation has distinct effects on each LC within a ganglion due to the underlying variability of K+ and Ca2+ currents in each cell.

We suggest that 5HT modulation has distinct effects on each LC within a ganglion due to the underlying variability of K+ and Ca2+ currents in each cell, and yet because 5HT has no effect on coupling this results in distinct hyperexcitable outputs from each cell that manifests as loss of synchronous activity.
